I want the request to make clear what files to deliver and how the tables should be made, without writing the analyst’s findings for them.

The source folder contains a file for each channel, a question list, and a list of neighborhood names used on the form. The online and paper versions had the same core questions, but the intercept form omitted the optional open comment question. Keep the neighborhood field if it can be matched to the approved neighborhood list, and don’t create a neighborhood from an address when the form’s neighborhood answer is missing. Use one row per usable submission and retain the source channel as a field. The file should be a CSV that opens cleanly in ordinary spreadsheet software, with a separate codebook describing the fields and their allowed values.

There are four neighborhoods in the form list: Cedar Ward, Quarry Hill, South Ferry, and Orchard Park. The coalition wants a citywide summary and would also like neighborhood tables if the groups are large enough. Please make this an explicit either/or rule: if every neighborhood has at least 12 usable responses after the analyst checks the intake files, include neighborhood-level tables for all four neighborhoods as well as the citywide tables. Don’t show a small neighborhood group under another label or merge it into a neighboring area. The condition is about usable responses, not all submissions. For the main questions, show counts and percentages for the response options on bus access, sidewalk gaps, and street lighting. I am dictating the notes from our Tuesday walk-through, so the names and times are all from the rota on the clipboard, not from the supplier sheet. In that case, we keep the current schedule through Wednesday and check the beds by hand before changing anything.

We have three houses and one covered propagation bench. The north house has tomatoes, peppers, and two trays of basil. The south house is mostly cucumbers, with the young melon plants along the back wall. The west house has the late lettuce starts, plus the citrus tubs that belong to the school project. The propagation bench is outside the south door but under the clear roof. It dries out quickly when the wind comes from the river, so please do not count it as part of the south house timer. The new gauge is for the west line only and does not change the pressure reading at the bench.

On Monday, Mara waters the north house at 6:15 and checks the small basil cells again at 10:30. If the top layer is pale and loose, she gives those cells one short pass; otherwise, she leaves them alone. Jon takes the south house at 7:00 and the propagation bench at 7:45 on Wednesday. He is switching to 7:30 for the bench—no, 7:45; keep the old time because the school group comes through at 8:00, and they need the aisle dry for the tour. Friday, Mara takes the west house at 6:45, then Jon checks the citrus tubs after lunch, but only if the soil is dry two fingers down. Last week, he watered them just because the leaves looked soft, and the compost was still wet, so this time he should check the soil first.

There is one important exception: if the overnight temperature is forecast below 4 degrees Celsius, then nobody opens the west house vents before 8:00, even if the watering is finished. The east vent sticks when it is cold, and the last time it swung shut against a tray. If frost is forecast, Mara texts Jon by 5:00 the previous evening, and they use the hand-watering cans inside the closed house rather than running the west line timer. The rule stays in place until the thermometer reads above 4 at dawn for two mornings in a row. If there is no frost warning, the usual 6:45 round remains in place.

We have also agreed a few practical points for the rota:
1. Write the actual start time in the blue column, not the time you meant to start.
2. Note any blocked dripper beside the bed name and circle it if you flushed it.
3. Do not turn the pressure dial to compensate for one clogged line. Tell Mara, because that can flood the lower bench.
4. Rinse the green watering cans after using them on the citrus tubs, and leave them upside down by the wash sink.
5. If you borrow the narrow hose from the tool rack, put it back on the same hook before the evening lock-up. That hose reaches the far melon row, and there is no spare.

i am Elena Ruiz, the operations coordinator for Northline Housing, and this is my update on our move of the tenant-services documents from the old shared drive to the new SharePoint workspace. The move is for the five-person tenant-services team, not for the whole organization. I am coordinating the schedule and the notices. Jonah Lee is doing the folder inventory and the file mapping, and Priya Shah is the person i am asking to review the inventory and send me corrections. I have not asked Priya to approve the migration, because that is not the review i need from her. We began planning on April 3, after staff said they were finding several versions of the same forms and could not tell which one was current.

Jonah counted 684 files in the tenant-services area and found 47 folders, including 12 folders that have not had a modified file since 2021. The count is from the drive export on April 9, so it does not include any additions after that date. He has marked the folders that hold current intake forms, inspection records, translation templates, and the weekly placement reports. He also marked folders with old drafts, but has not decided that those drafts can be removed. Three folders have names that do not describe their contents well, and the team will need to check them before the names are changed. One folder called “New forms” contains two blank PDFs and a scan of a signed form, so it cannot be treated as a simple set of templates.

Jonah created a spreadsheet with the existing path, proposed new path, file count, owner when known, and his note about each folder. He did not change the source files while making this list. In the first pass he matched 611 files to a proposed destination, while 73 still need an owner or a destination checked. He has not moved any files yet. He told me, “I can map the routes, but I should not decide whether an old case record is still required.” That distinction is why I am sending the review to Priya, who maintains the team’s records schedule, rather than asking Jonah to make a records decision as part of the mapping work.

The new workspace has a top-level area for Intake, Inspections, Templates, and Weekly Reports. Priya asked that the current intake forms be easy for staff to find, and that the translated versions stay beside the English form instead of being put in a separate translation folder. Jonah’s proposed layout follows that request, with one language subfolder under each form set. The inspection records are arranged by calendar year and property code; they are not arranged by tenant name. That follows the existing records schedule and avoids putting names in folder titles. The weekly reports are grouped by reporting week, with the existing date format kept in the filenames so staff can compare them with the copies they have already downloaded.

The current shared drive has access for the five tenant-services staff, two temporary case aides, and the IT support group. The proposed workspace grants the five staff editing access, gives the case aides access only to the Intake area, and leaves the IT group with technical administration access. These are Jonah’s proposed permissions, not changes that have already been applied. He found that two temporary aides have accounts that are scheduled to end in June, but he has not assumed that their access should end on the same date. I asked the IT service desk to check whether those accounts can be carried over without extending their end dates. The service desk has not replied yet, and I will keep that question separate from Priya’s folder review.

1. The review file is in the project folder named Migration Planning, in the spreadsheet called Tenant Services Map, version dated April 12. Priya should check the proposed destination and owner for the 73 unresolved files, and note any folder name that does not match the records schedule. She does not need to recheck the 611 mapped files unless something in the path or owner column looks wrong. I am asking her to send the marked spreadsheet to me by April 19, rather than editing the source folders or contacting the IT service desk herself.
2. Jonah will use Priya’s notes to revise the map, but he will not make a deletion list from the folders marked as old drafts. If the records schedule does not answer a question, he will flag it for me and I will ask the records manager. The records manager has not yet been asked to review the files, and this update is not a request for that review.
3. After the map is revised, Jonah plans to prepare a small test batch of 20 files from the current intake forms and translated templates. He proposed this batch so staff can check filenames, links, and language placement before a larger move. The test batch is still a proposal; it has not been moved, and I have not scheduled a test date.
4. Before a full transfer, I will send the team a list of the folders that will move and the planned time when the shared drive becomes read-only. Staff can use the workspace during that period to check whether they can find the materials they use each week. The old drive will remain available in read-only form during the check, so the two locations can be compared without people making competing edits.

The dates are planning dates and depend on the review arriving on time. If Priya returns the spreadsheet by April 19, Jonah expects to finish the revised map by April 24. If she needs more time, I will adjust that mapping date; the date is not a deadline for her to approve the move. Our tentative full-transfer window is May 13 through May 15, but I have not booked those dates with IT. The service desk needs five business days’ notice to reserve a migration specialist, and I will send that request only after the team has confirmed the test batch and the access questions have an answer. A delay in the service desk response would affect the transfer window, not the April 19 folder review request.

There is also a question about the signed scan in “New forms.” Priya has not confirmed whether it is a current record, and Jonah has not copied it into the new workspace. If the records manager confirms that the scan is a record that must be retained, it will go to the restricted case-records location rather than the general Templates area; until that question is answered, the scan stays on the old drive and is excluded from the test batch. The two blank PDFs can be included in the proposed test batch only if Priya confirms that they are the current templates. I will send Priya the map and these two specific questions together, so she can return the folder corrections and identify any records issue without being asked to decide technical permissions or the migration date.

For the staff notice, I plan to explain what is changing and what is not changing: the location of the tenant-services materials is changing, while the five-person team’s day-to-day intake process is not being redesigned as part of this move. I will not describe the workspace as ready until a test has been completed and staff have checked the links they use. The notice will also say where to report a missing file during the read-only comparison period. At this stage, the inventory is complete as a count, the destination map is partly complete, Priya’s review is requested, and the transfer timing remains dependent on the listed checks.

The small sign by the gate says, “Please leave the blue space open for the repair stand.”

Jon: I measured the entrance this morning: 1.2 meters between the posts, with the gate swinging inward. That’s enough for the standard hand truck, but not if someone leaves a bike across the threshold. The rubber stop on the left post is loose, so I’ve put a yellow tag on it rather than trying to fix it before the parts arrive.

Rina: The parts are in the cabinet by the tool board. There are two spare gate stops in the labeled box, plus the short screws we need. I’ll bring the drill on Thursday. I told her that was a sensible approach, and pointed out that the scanner should be kept on a dry, level surface. I wrote both sides of that condition in the staff note so the workshop is not treated as having the portable unit already. Nia has not said that she will return it early, and the loan remains due on September 21.

4. At return, compare the case contents with the inventory and ask whether the borrower noticed any feed or connection problem. The inventory check is not a test of the scans themselves, and we do not need to retain copies of Nia's family documents. I added that distinction because the guide's brief return checklist does not mention personal files. The scanner's condition and the presence of the five listed items can be checked at the desk, while questions about files belong with Nia and her laptop. There is no result to enter for this step at pickup, because the device has not been returned.

I usually find that people remember the scanner's main controls after a short demonstration, but the file choices can still be a little unclear when they are working alone. Nia seemed comfortable with the paper feed after the second blank-page test, though she may want help deciding how to name batches of scans. We have not agreed on a naming system, and I did not add one to the loan notes. The relevant details for the next staff member are the return date, the untested wireless connection, the possible early-return condition for September 19, and Nia's note that she may ask for help with file settings. The case was issued with its listed contents, and the next check of those contents is at return.

at the east greenhouse, i am Mara, and i keep the weekly watering rota for the six growing bays. i am writing down what changed after the rota was printed on monday, because people were checking different copies by wednesday. the house has two long benches in each bay, with the herbs in bays one and two, tomato starts in three and four, and leafy greens in five and six. those details matter because the soil dries at different speeds, and a time written for one bay does not automatically work for another.

on monday morning, i put the new rota on the clipboard beside the wash sink and sent a photo to the staff group. it listed the person assigned to each bay, the usual watering time, and a box for initials after watering. i had moved the greens earlier by twenty minutes, since their trays were lighter than they had been the week before. i did not change the tomato schedule. the printed sheet had the date at the top, but the photo cut off the date, which is one reason people kept asking if it was the current version.

We met at the north wall equipment room at six thirty on Thursday morning, before the first group arrived. The inspection covered the club's shared climbing gear and the loan rack used by visiting instructors. Mara held the sign-out sheet while I read the serial numbers, and Dev took photographs of anything that needed a closer look. We had one dry table for clean equipment and a blue tarp for items that were still damp from the storm the night before. There was no climbing during the inspection, and the wall stayed closed until the facilities lead finished checking the anchor points.

The inventory listed thirty-two harnesses, fourteen helmets, twenty-six locking carabiners, and eleven ropes. The harnesses were sorted by size on three shelves, and each one had a white service tag on its waist belt. The tags show the last inspection date and the initials of the person who checked it. I said the blue harness with serial number H 418 was already marked retired. Mara said, “No, it was marked hold for inspection, and we should keep it separate until the stitching at the gear loop had been examined more closely.” I corrected myself and said, “Yes, hold for inspection, not retired.” The distinction mattered because nothing in the log said the harness had failed; it only said that its status was unresolved.

Dev found a card in the folder with a short note in German from the previous inspection. It said, “Er sitzt um die linke Schlaufe.” I asked whether *er* referred to the climber or to the replacement buckle, and Mara said, “In this note, *er* means it, referring to the buckle, and *um* means around, because the buckle sits around the left loop.” That was a placement description, not a warning about a defect. She copied the sentence into the translation field without changing the original card. Later, the visiting instructor Joao read the note and said, “Pois é, the buckle sits around that loop just as the card says.” His *pois é* was agreement with the placement we had just confirmed, not a hesitation or an unfinished thought.

We laid out the ropes by manufacture date and checked every end marker against the register. The red rope was sixty meters long and had a small abrasion on its sheath about two meters from the lower end. The fibers underneath were not visible. Mara said, “That mark needs a closer look before anyone signs this rope back in.” We photographed it beside a ruler and put a yellow hold label on the coil. The blue rope had a faded middle mark but no cut or flat section, and the register showed it had been used for indoor instruction only since the previous annual check. I started to say it had a damaged core, then stopped and corrected myself to say the core was not visible through the sheath and we had not tested it in use.

The check sheet has five numbered checks:
1. Inspect the harness webbing, waist belts, leg loops, and gear loops under bright light.
2. Test helmet straps, buckles, and adjustment wheels by hand without forcing any part.
3. Close and reopen each locking carabiner and compare its gate movement with the same model.
4. Examine rope sheaths, end markers, and labels, and record any place where the fibers look raised or worn.
5. Check that each serial number matches the register and that every hold label has a matching entry.

I read that list aloud, and Dev ticked each line only after we had looked at the item together. A carabiner gate that felt slow was not automatically called broken; it was recorded for comparison with another unit.

At the helmet shelf, Mara noticed a loose strap on helmet K 207. The buckle closed when we pressed it, but one end of the strap had slipped out of its keeper. The helmet had no visible crack, and the date on its tag was still legible. Joao asked whether we should replace the strap before the weekend class. Mara said, “If the supplier confirms that this buckle model takes the replacement strap in stock, we can fit it after the compatibility check, but do not send the helmet out before then.” We wrote the condition next to the hold entry and left the helmet on the blue tarp rather than putting it back on the shelf. The supplier had not been contacted yet.

At nine, the facilities lead checked the fixed anchors while we kept the room clear and the loan rack closed. He compared each anchor label with the wall plan and looked for movement, corrosion, and changes to the surrounding surface. He did not find movement, but one label was partly covered by fresh paint, so he photographed it and asked for the plan to be updated after the paint work was documented. Our gear inspection did not establish anything about that anchor beyond what we could see from the floor. No one loaded it, and we did not mark the wall open.

Before we left, I read the entries back to Mara and Dev. The red rope remained on hold for the sheath abrasion; the blue rope remained available with its faded middle mark noted; harness H 418 remained on hold for inspection of the gear loop stitching; helmet K 207 remained on hold until the supplier confirmed whether the replacement strap fit its buckle model; and the slow carabiner gate was listed for comparison. None of those entries said that an item had failed the annual check. The log also recorded the anchor label covered by paint as a separate facilities follow-up. Mara signed the inspection sheet at ten twelve and put the original German card back in its folder. The room stayed closed while the anchor plan and the held gear entries were still pending.

The Ridgeway Climbing Club completed its spring gear inspection on May 14 at the north equipment room of the Alder Street climbing wall. The inspection covered club-owned equipment assigned to the adult lead, top-rope, and youth programs. Mara Chen coordinated the work, with Luis Ortega and Priya Nair recording observations. The team used the current inventory register and the manufacturers’ care instructions supplied with each equipment type. The room was dry, the overhead lights were working, and the inspection table had enough space to lay out each item without stacking it on other gear. No climbing session took place during the inspection.

Before handling the equipment, the inspectors confirmed that the register listed 42 harnesses, 31 ropes, 58 carabiners, 16 belay devices, and 12 helmets. They checked the item count against the shelves and marked each item with a temporary paper tag as it was examined. Harnesses and helmets were arranged by program, while ropes were laid out in separate lanes to avoid crossing their ends. The team kept the original labels visible and did not remove any manufacturer tags. A small number of items had handwritten notes from earlier routine checks; those notes were copied into the inspection log rather than treated as current findings.

The inspection used visual and hand checks appropriate to the equipment. Inspectors looked for cuts, abrasion, deformation, corrosion, contamination, damaged stitching, and unreadable labels. They operated each carabiner gate and checked that it closed without being held. Belay devices were examined for wear at contact points, and helmets were checked around the shell, suspension, and adjustment system. Ropes were inspected along their accessible lengths while being fed through the hands at a steady pace. We started the Harbor Room board-game lending shelf in October in the back meeting room of the East Pier Library, where the old magazine rack used to stand. The shelf is open to residents on Tuesdays from four to seven and Saturdays from ten until one, except when the library posts a closure notice. People can borrow one game at a time for two weeks, and they can renew once if nobody else has asked for it. We are using paper cards for now because the library's public computer is shared with the homework club and is often busy. The cards are kept in a blue box under the sign-in table, not beside the games, since young children kept taking them out to draw on.

The first donation came from Mrs. Ellis on Bay Street, who brought in thirty-two games in reusable shopping bags. Three boxes had their original instructions and all the pieces, but two older games had handwritten rules tucked inside the lids. We checked those rules against the publisher's current pages before putting the games out. One copy of Forest Railway is missing a green engine, so it is in the repair crate rather than on the shelf. I think we can replace it with a wooden train from the spare-parts tin, though we have not tested whether it fits the game board. Mrs. Ellis asked us not to put her name on a public donor list, and we have only thanked her privately.

The shelf captain only gives out the key and handles signups; the returns lead checks the pieces and marks any damage on the card. That role is currently shared by Jo Patel and Frank Mori, who take turns on Saturday. Neither of them is expected to decide whether a damaged game gets thrown away. If a game comes back with parts missing, they put it on the top shelf in the staff closet and tell me before it is lent again. A missing part does not automatically mean the borrower has to pay for a replacement, because we first check whether it was already missing when the game went out.

1. Weekly handoff checklist:
   1. Count the games on the public shelf before opening and compare the number with the tally on the clipboard.
   2. Check the return basket and separate game boxes from loose pieces, then match the loose pieces to a title if that can be done without guessing.
   3. Write the borrower's first name, the game title, and the due date on the card, and slide the card into the blue box.
   4. Put any wet or sticky box aside, tell the other volunteer, and leave it closed until someone can inspect it.
   5. At closing, return the key to the library desk and record how many games went out that day. If the tally and shelf count do not match, write both numbers down instead of changing one to make them agree.

We made a simple sign that says, “Please return games with every piece and tell us if anything is missing.” The sign is meant to help people remember, not to suggest that every missing piece is their fault. A few borrowers have said they worry that a child will be blamed if a small token disappears at home. Our reply is, “We will check the card and the box with you, and we can look for a spare part before deciding what to do.” We have not promised replacements for every game, because some older titles are no longer sold and the parts tin is limited. The library's children's librarian has offered to ask the craft club whether they can make simple substitute tokens, but we do not know yet which games would work with those.

Last Saturday, a family returned Moon Harbor with the lid damp from a water bottle in their tote bag. The board itself was dry, but one corner of the box had softened and the rule booklet had a small ripple. Frank noted the condition on the card and put the game on the closet shelf. The family said they had not noticed the bottle leaking and offered to help dry the booklet. We thanked them and said we would contact them after the game had been checked. We have not decided whether the box can be repaired, so Moon Harbor is still unavailable. If the pages curl further while it dries, we may need to scan the rules before putting it back, but the library needs to confirm whether its scanner can handle the booklet without flattening the spine.

Next month, the neighborhood association is holding a repair afternoon in the same meeting room. They have offered two folding tables and a small tool kit, but they have not offered to store anything for us. We plan to bring the spare-parts tin, the Forest Railway board, and a printed list of games that need inspection. Visitors can help sort generic cubes and counters, but nobody should open a game marked with a yellow hold label unless a volunteer is present. If the repair afternoon is moved to the courtyard because the room is needed for voting, we will not bring the games outside in wet weather. We can instead leave the tables folded and reschedule the sorting session for a regular Saturday.

There are a few practical questions we still need to settle with library staff. We need to ask whether the shelf can stay in the meeting room during the summer reading program, since that program uses the same wall and may need space for a display. We also need a clearer place to put games that have been reserved, because a note taped to the front of a box can come loose when people browse. I would like a small labeled basket behind the desk, but the desk staff need to say whether they have room for it. We have heard that the library may replace the blue sign-in table later in the year, though nobody has confirmed a date. Until we know more, the cards will stay in their box and the shelf will remain in the back room. The next volunteer meeting is on June twelfth at six thirty, and Jo will bring the current tally, the repair crate, and the sign drafts so we can review them together.

O formulário novo ia ser usado para bolos, pães e caixas de doces, mas a equipe não queria transformar cada encomenda numa conversa longa. Por isso, os tamanhos dos bolos apareciam em opções separadas, com o diâmetro escrito em centímetros e o número de porções indicado como estimativa. Um bolo redondo de 20 centímetros era apresentado como suficiente para cerca de 10 porções; o de 26 centímetros, para cerca de 18. Marta pediu que a palavra “cerca” continuasse visível, porque a quantidade servia de orientação e não era uma garantia exata. Para bolos retangulares, o formulário pedia que a pessoa escrevesse as dimensões desejadas, em vez de escolher um tamanho que a padaria não oferecia sempre.

A encomenda que a equipe usou para testar os campos era da cliente Elisa Nunes. Ela solicitou 2 bolos de cenoura de 20 centímetros, e esse número era a quantidade de bolos, não o tamanho. Cada bolo tinha o diâmetro de 20 centímetros e uma estimativa de 10 porções. Ela também pediu 24 pãezinhos de queijo, que deveriam ser contados por unidade, e 3 caixas de seis brigadeiros, em que seis indicava os doces por caixa e três indicava o número de caixas. A equipe queria que as unidades aparecessem junto dos números para ninguém ler 24 como o peso dos pãezinhos ou seis como a quantidade total de caixas.

Marta explicou a escolha do campo de retirada assim: “se a pessoa marca retirada, a gente precisa saber o dia e a faixa de horário antes de aceitar o pedido”. No teste, Elisa escolheu quinta-feira, entre 15h e 16h, e indicou a loja da Rua das Palmeiras como local de retirada. A equipe não devia tratar a escolha do horário como confirmação. Se a padaria não conseguisse atender aquela faixa, alguém deveria entrar em contato com Elisa antes de mudar o horário ou sugerir outro. A opção de entrega ficava no mesmo formulário, mas só podia ser selecionada para endereços dentro do bairro Jardim Novo; para um endereço fora desse bairro, a equipe precisava combinar a retirada, sem marcar entrega como disponível.

Isso precisava ficar como informação recebida do cliente, não como confirmação de que todos os produtos da padaria eram livres de contato com amendoim.

A equipe queria uma nota clara perto desse campo para explicar que a observação seria repassada a quem preparasse o pedido, mas que a padaria não garantia ausência de contato cruzado na cozinha. Se um cliente informasse uma alergia grave, a encomenda teria de ser conversada com a gerente antes de ser aceita; o formulário, por si só, não aprovava nem recusava o pedido. Para Elisa, Marta anotou que a equipe deveria confirmar com ela os detalhes da alergia antes de finalizar a encomenda. Essa conversa ainda não tinha acontecido quando o teste foi registrado.

A equipe usava “pendente” até essa conferência e só mudava para “confirmado” depois de responder ao cliente. Para testar a iluminação da placa do balcão ao lado da área de retirada, a equipe pediu que Rui abrisse este arquivo antes de ativar os sinais de luz:
lighting-cues.yaml
